questions.question: Which of the following best explains the term 'formula unit mass'?

options.text: The mass of one mole of a substance
The mass of a single atom of an element
The mass of a single molecule of an element
The total mass of all atoms in one formula unit of a compound

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The total mass of all atoms in one formula unit of a compound**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The term **formula unit mass** refers to the **total mass of all the atoms in one formula unit of a compound**. It is expressed in atomic mass units (amu).
 
• A **formula unit** represents the simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound. For example, in NaCl, one formula unit consists of one sodium ion (Na⁺) and one chloride ion (Cl⁻).
 
• The **formula unit mass** is calculated by summing the atomic masses of all atoms present in the chemical formula of the compound. For instance, in NaCl, the formula unit mass = atomic mass of Na + atomic mass of Cl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 amu.
 
• The formula unit mass is particularly used for **ionic compounds** because these do not exist as discrete molecules but as a lattice structure. Hence, the term "formula unit" is used instead of "molecule."
 
• This concept is essential in stoichiometry, allowing chemists to calculate the mass relationships in chemical reactions involving ionic compounds.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Atomic Mass:**

 
 
• The mass of an individual atom is expressed in atomic mass units (amu). For example, the atomic mass of sodium (Na) is approximately 23 amu, and that of chlorine (Cl) is 35.5 amu.
 
• The atomic mass is determined relative to the mass of one atom of carbon-12, which is defined as exactly 12 amu.
 
 
 
• **Formula Unit:**
 
 
• A formula unit is the smallest repeating unit of an ionic compound that represents its composition. For example, the formula unit of magnesium chloride is MgCl₂.
 
• It differs from a molecule because ionic compounds do not form discrete molecular entities but rather exist as a lattice of ions.
 
 
 
• **Difference Between Formula Unit Mass and Molecular Mass:**
 
 
• **Formula unit mass** is used for ionic compounds (e.g., NaCl, MgCl₂) and is based on the simplest ratio of ions.
 
• **Molecular mass** applies to covalent compounds (e.g., H₂O, CO₂) and is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Formula Unit Mass:**
 
 
• It helps in calculating molar mass, which is crucial for stoichiometric calculations in chemistry.
 
• It is used to determine the proportions of elements in ionic compounds and their chemical behavior.
 
 
 
• **Examples:**
 
 
• The formula unit mass of NaCl: 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 amu.
 
• The formula unit mass of MgCl₂: 24.3 + (2 × 35.5) = 95.3 amu.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1:** "The mass of one mole of a substance" refers to molar mass, not formula unit mass. **This is incorrect.**
 
• **Option 2:** "The mass of a single atom of an element" refers to atomic mass, not formula unit mass. **This is incorrect.**
 
• **Option 3:** "The mass of a single molecule of an element" pertains to molecular mass, which is different from formula unit mass. **This is incorrect.**
 
• **Option 4:** "The total mass of all atoms in one formula unit of a compound" is the correct definition of formula unit mass. **This is correct.**

questions.question: A convex lens has a focal length of 25 cm. What is the power of this convex lens?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**+4.0 D**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **power of a lens** is the ability of the lens to converge or diverge light rays passing through it. It is measured in **dioptres (D)**.
 
• The formula to calculate the power of a lens is:

 **P = 100 / f**, where **P** is the power in dioptres and **f** is the focal length in centimeters.
 
• In the given question, the focal length of the convex lens is **25 cm**. Substituting this into the formula:

 **P = 100 / 25 = +4.0 D**.
 
• A **positive power (+)** indicates that the lens is a **convex lens**, which converges light rays.
 
• Hence, the power of the convex lens is **+4.0 D**, and **this is the correct answer.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Convex Lens:**

 
 
• A convex lens is also known as a **converging lens** because it brings parallel rays of light to a focus.
 
• It is thicker at the center and thinner at the edges.
 
• Convex lenses are commonly used in devices like **magnifying glasses, cameras, and projectors**.
 
 
 
• **Dioptre:**
 
 
• The dioptre (D) is the unit of measurement for the optical power of a lens or a curved mirror.
 
• It is defined as the reciprocal of the focal length in meters (**D = 1/f**), where **f** is in meters.
 
• A positive dioptre value indicates a converging lens (convex), while a negative value indicates a diverging lens (concave).
 
 
 
• **Lens Power and Focal Length:**
 
 
• The focal length (**f**) of a lens is the distance from the center of the lens to the point where light rays converge or diverge.
 
• The shorter the focal length, the higher the optical power of the lens.
 
• For example, a lens with a focal length of 50 cm has a power of **+2.0 D**, while a lens with a focal length of 25 cm has a power of **+4.0 D**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Convex Lenses:**
 
 
• Convex lenses are used in **eyeglasses** to correct farsightedness (hyperopia).
 
• They are also used in **microscopes** and **telescopes** for magnification purposes.
 
• Other applications include their use in **optical instruments**, cameras, and focusing systems.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Power of Concave Lens:**

 
 
• A concave lens is a **diverging lens**, and its power is represented by a **negative** value.
 
• For example, if the focal length of a concave lens is 50 cm, its power is **-2.0 D**.
 
 
 
• **Difference Between Convex and Concave Lenses:**
 
 
• **Convex Lens:** Converges light rays, has positive power, and is thicker at the center.
 
• **Concave Lens:** Diverges light rays, has negative power, and is thinner at the center.
 
 
 
• **Real and Virtual Images:**
 
 
• A convex lens can form both **real and virtual images**, depending on the position of the object.
 
• A concave lens, however, always forms a **virtual image**.

questions.question: Which type of meristematic tissue is responsible for increase in the height of plants?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Apical meristem**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Apical meristem** is a type of meristematic tissue found at the **tips of roots and shoots** in plants.
 
• It is responsible for the **primary growth** of plants, leading to an **increase in height** or length.
 
• The cells in the apical meristem are actively dividing and undifferentiated, enabling the elongation of stems and roots.
 
• Apical meristems give rise to three primary meristems: **protoderm (epidermis), procambium (vascular tissues), and ground meristem (ground tissues)**.
 
• This tissue ensures that plants grow taller or deeper by adding new cells at the apex of the plant body.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Secondary meristem:**

 
 
• This type of meristematic tissue is responsible for **secondary growth**, which leads to an increase in the **thickness or girth** of the plant body.
 
• Examples include the **vascular cambium** and **cork cambium**.
 
• It is found in woody plants and contributes to the formation of bark and wood.
 
 
 
• **Cambium:**
 
 
• Cambium is a type of secondary meristem that specifically produces **vascular tissues** like xylem and phloem.
 
• It is responsible for the **lateral growth** of plants, increasing the width of stems and roots.
 
• It is not involved in the increase in height but plays a crucial role in the plant's strength and transport system.
 
 
 
• **Lateral meristem:**
 
 
• Lateral meristems are located along the sides of stems and roots.
 
• Their function is to contribute to **secondary growth** by increasing the diameter or thickness of the plant body.
 
• Examples of lateral meristems include **vascular cambium** and **cork cambium**.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• **Meristematic tissues** are responsible for the growth of plants due to their ability to divide continuously.
 
• Meristems are classified based on their **location** (apical, lateral, intercalary) and **function** (primary or secondary growth).
 
• **Apical dominance:** The apical bud suppresses the growth of lateral buds, ensuring that the plant grows upwards efficiently.
 
• Plants with active apical meristems typically exhibit **elongation of roots and stems**, allowing them to explore new areas for nutrients, water, and light.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is NOT true about average speed?

options.text: Average speed only needs the magnitude, not direction
Its SI unit is metres per second m/s
To find speed, we need both the magnitude and direction of the object
Speed is calculated as distance divided by time

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To find speed, we need both the magnitude and direction of the object.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1:** "Average speed only needs the magnitude, not direction" – This statement is correct. **Average speed** is a scalar quantity, meaning it is only concerned with the magnitude of distance traveled over time and does not consider direction.
 
• **Statement 2:** "Its SI unit is metres per second (m/s)" – This statement is correct. The **SI unit** of speed, including average speed, is **metres per second (m/s)**, as it is derived from the formula of speed: distance (metres) divided by time (seconds).
 
• **Statement 3:** "To find speed, we need both the magnitude and direction of the object" – This statement is incorrect. Speed is a **scalar quantity**, and it does not depend on direction. If direction is included, it becomes velocity, which is a vector quantity. This is the correct answer as it is NOT true.__
 
• **Statement 4:** "Speed is calculated as distance divided by time" – This statement is correct. The formula for speed is indeed **distance ÷ time**, which gives the rate at which an object covers distance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Difference Between Speed and Velocity:**

 
 
• **Speed:** Speed is a scalar quantity that measures how fast an object is moving. It considers only the magnitude of the motion.
 
• **Velocity:** Velocity is a vector quantity that measures the rate of displacement of an object in a specific direction. It considers both magnitude and direction.
 
• Example: If a car travels 50 km north in one hour, the **speed** is 50 km/h, while the **velocity** is 50 km/h north.
 
 
 
• **Formula for Average Speed:**
 
 
• **Average Speed = Total Distance / Total Time**
 
• It does not take into account the direction of travel, making it different from average velocity.
 
 
 
• **SI Unit of Speed:**
 
 
• The **SI unit** of speed is **metres per second (m/s)**.
 
• For practical purposes, speed is often measured in **kilometres per hour (km/h)** in daily life.
 
 
 
• **Uniform and Non-Uniform Motion:**
 
 
• **Uniform Motion:** When an object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, it is said to be in uniform motion. In this case, the speed remains constant.
 
• **Non-Uniform Motion:** When an object covers unequal distances in equal intervals of time, it is said to be in non-uniform motion. The speed varies in this case.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Speed in Real Life:**
 
 
• Speed is used in transportation to measure how fast vehicles move.
 
• It is crucial in sports, especially in events like running and racing.
 
• Speed measurements are used in industries like aviation and shipping for navigation and logistics.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Scalar vs. Vector Quantities:**

 
 
• **Scalar:** Quantities that have only magnitude (e.g., speed, distance, time).
 
• **Vector:** Quantities that have both magnitude and direction (e.g., velocity, displacement, force).
 
 
 
• **Examples of Speed and Velocity:**
 
 
• If a person runs 100 meters in 10 seconds, their speed is **10 m/s**.
 
• If the same person runs 100 meters north in 10 seconds, their velocity is **10 m/s north**.

questions.question: Which of the following shows acidic behaviour in aqueous solution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**HCl**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Acidic behavior in aqueous solutions:** Acids are substances that release **hydrogen ions (H⁺)** when dissolved in water. The presence of H⁺ ions is responsible for the acidic nature of a solution.
 
• **HCl (Hydrochloric Acid):** HCl is a strong acid that completely dissociates in water, releasing a high concentration of hydrogen ions (H⁺). This dissociation contributes to the acidic behavior of HCl in aqueous solutions.
 
• **Ca(OH)₂, NaOH, and KOH:** These are strong bases that dissociate in water to release hydroxide ions (OH⁻), which neutralize hydrogen ions. Hence, they exhibit basic rather than acidic behavior in aqueous solutions.
 
• Acidity is measured using the **pH scale**: Solutions with a pH less than 7 are acidic. HCl solutions typically have a very low pH due to the high concentration of H⁺ ions.
 
• **Example:** In laboratories, HCl is commonly used as an acid for various chemical reactions, demonstrating its strong acidic properties.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Hydrochloric Acid (HCl):**

 
 
• HCl is a **strong monoprotic acid**, meaning it can donate one proton (H⁺) per molecule.
 
• It is widely used in industries for applications such as **metal cleaning, pH adjustment, and chemical synthesis**.
 
• Its molecular formula is HCl, and its aqueous solution is commonly referred to as **hydrogen chloride.**
 
• In the human body, HCl is produced in the stomach to aid digestion by breaking down food and killing pathogens.
 
 
 
• **Calcium Hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂):**
 
 
• Also known as **slaked lime**, it is a strong base and used in industries for **neutralizing acids** and **water purification**.
 
• It dissociates in water to release hydroxide ions (OH⁻), making the solution basic.
 
• Commonly used in construction as a component of mortar and plaster.
 
 
 
• **Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH):**
 
 
• NaOH, or **caustic soda**, is a strong base used in the manufacture of soap, paper, and textiles.
 
• It dissociates completely in water to produce hydroxide ions, contributing to its basic behavior.
 
• It is highly corrosive and must be handled with care.
 
 
 
• **Potassium Hydroxide (KOH):**
 
 
• KOH, commonly known as **caustic potash**, is a strong base used in fertilizers, soaps, and batteries.
 
• It releases hydroxide ions in aqueous solutions, leading to basic properties.
 
• It is also used in laboratories for titrations and chemical synthesis.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Acid-Base Behavior:**

 
 
• Acids release **H⁺ ions** in water, while bases release **OH⁻ ions**.
 
• Strong acids like HCl fully dissociate in water, whereas weak acids partially dissociate.
 
• Strong bases like NaOH and KOH also fully dissociate in aqueous solutions.
 
 
 
• **pH Scale:**
 
 
• The **pH scale** ranges from 0 to 14, with values below 7 indicating acidic solutions and values above 7 indicating basic solutions.
 
• Neutral solutions have a pH of 7, such as pure water.
 
• HCl solutions typically have a pH of 1 to 3, depending on the concentration.
 
 
 
• **Applications:**
 
 
• HCl is used in laboratory experiments, industrial processes, and medical applications.
 
• Bases like NaOH and KOH are utilized in manufacturing, cleaning, and analytical procedures.
 
• Ca(OH)₂ is commonly used in agriculture to neutralize acidic soils.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding loudness of sound?

options.text: Loudness depends on the speed of wave.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Loudness depends on the amplitude.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Loudness of sound** primarily depends on the **amplitude** of the sound wave. The larger the amplitude, the louder the sound perceived.
 
• Amplitude refers to the maximum displacement of particles in a medium due to the propagation of a sound wave. A higher amplitude causes greater energy transfer, resulting in a louder sound.
 
• The **frequency** of a sound wave determines the pitch, not loudness. Hence, the statement "Loudness depends on frequency" is **incorrect**.
 
• The **speed of the wave** is determined by the medium through which the sound travels and does not affect loudness. Therefore, the statement "Loudness depends on the speed of wave" is **incorrect**.
 
• **Wavelength** is inversely proportional to frequency in sound waves and does not directly affect loudness. Thus, the statement "Loudness depends on the wavelength" is **incorrect**.
 
• Loudness is also influenced by the sensitivity of the human ear and the duration of exposure to sound.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Amplitude:**

 
 
• Amplitude is measured in units like **decibels (dB)**, which quantify the intensity of sound.
 
• For example, a typical conversation has an amplitude of about **60 dB**, while a jet engine can reach over **120 dB**.
 
• Higher amplitudes correspond to louder sounds, whereas lower amplitudes are associated with softer sounds.
 
 
 
• **Frequency:**
 
 
• Frequency is measured in **Hertz (Hz)** and determines the pitch of the sound.
 
• Humans can typically hear frequencies in the range of **20 Hz to 20,000 Hz**, with higher frequencies perceived as higher-pitched sounds.
 
• While pitch and loudness are distinct qualities, they often interact in perception.
 
 
 
• **Speed of Sound:**
 
 
• The speed of sound varies with the medium, e.g., **343 m/s** in air, **1,500 m/s** in water, and **5,960 m/s** in steel.
 
• Factors like temperature, pressure, and density of the medium influence the speed of sound.
 
• However, the speed does not directly impact loudness.
 
 
 
• **Wavelength:**
 
 
• Wavelength is the distance between successive crests or troughs in a sound wave.
 
• It is inversely proportional to frequency, as per the equation: **wavelength = speed of sound / frequency**.
 
• Like frequency, wavelength contributes to the tonal quality rather than loudness.
 
 
 
• **Human Ear Sensitivity:**
 
 
• The human ear is most sensitive to frequencies between **2,000 Hz and 5,000 Hz**, where small changes in amplitude result in significant changes in perceived loudness.
 
• Prolonged exposure to loud sounds above **85 dB** can cause hearing damage.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Threshold of Hearing:**

 
 
• The quietest sound a human can hear is at **0 dB**, known as the threshold of hearing.
 
• Sounds above **120 dB** are painful and can cause immediate hearing loss.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Loudness Measurement:**
 
 
• Loudness is essential in audio engineering, designing sound systems, and acoustics.
 
• Devices like **sound level meters** are used to measure amplitude for safety and environmental purposes.
 
 
 
• **Noise Pollution:**
 
 
• Excessive loudness contributes to noise pollution, which can lead to health issues like **stress, sleep disturbances, and hearing impairment**.
 
• Regulations often enforce limits on noise levels in residential and industrial areas.
 
 
 
• **Equal Loudness Contours:**
 
 
• These are graphs showing the sound pressure levels required to produce the same perceived loudness at different frequencies.
 
• They highlight the frequency-dependent sensitivity of the human ear.

questions.question: Work done by a constant force is zero if:

options.text: displacement is zero or perpendicular to force

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Work done by a constant force is zero if displacement is zero or perpendicular to force.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Definition of Work:** Work is defined as the product of the force applied on an object and the displacement of the object in the direction of the force. Mathematically, **Work (W) = F × d × cos(θ)**, where:

 
 
• **F** is the magnitude of the applied force.
 
• **d** is the magnitude of displacement.
 
• **θ** is the angle between the force and displacement vectors.
 
 
 
• **Condition for Zero Work:** The work done by a constant force is zero when:
 
 
• **Displacement (d) = 0:** If the object does not move (no displacement), the work done is zero because W = F × 0 × cos(θ) = 0.
 
• **Force and Displacement are Perpendicular (θ = 90°):** When the angle between the force and displacement is 90°, cos(90°) = 0, leading to W = F × d × 0 = 0.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Zero Work:**
 
 
• A person holding a heavy box stationary does no work because there is no displacement.
 
• A satellite moving in a circular orbit under the influence of gravitational force does no work because the force is perpendicular to the displacement.
 
 
 
• **Relevance of the Formula:** The formula W = F × d × cos(θ) clearly shows that work depends on both the displacement and the angle between the force and displacement. If either displacement is zero or the angle is 90°, the work becomes zero.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Work:**

 
 
• Work is a scalar quantity, meaning it has magnitude but no direction.
 
• Positive work occurs when force and displacement are in the same direction (θ = 0°, cos(0°) = 1).
 
• Negative work occurs when force and displacement are in opposite directions (θ = 180°, cos(180°) = -1).
 
 
 
• **Concept of Force and Displacement:**
 
 
• For work to occur, there must be a displacement in the direction of the applied force.
 
• If there is no displacement, such as in static scenarios, no work is done regardless of the force applied.
 
 
 
• **Work Done in Perpendicular Scenarios:**
 
 
• When force is perpendicular to displacement, the angle θ is 90°, and cos(90°) = 0, leading to zero work.
 
• Examples: A person carrying a bag while walking horizontally (force exerted vertically while displacement is horizontal).
 
 
 
• **Practical Applications:**
 
 
• Understanding zero work is important in designing systems like pulleys and levers where forces need to be perpendicular to avoid unnecessary work.
 
• In physics problems, identifying cases of zero work helps simplify calculations and understand energy conservation principles.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1: Displacement is small**

 
 
• Even if the displacement is small, work is done as long as there is a component of force in the direction of displacement.
 
• **Incorrect**, as zero work depends on the angle and displacement being zero, not its magnitude.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: Force is large**
 
 
• The magnitude of force alone does not determine zero work.
 
• **Incorrect**, as work depends on both force and displacement.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: Force is variable**
 
 
• Variable force affects the calculation of work but does not inherently result in zero work.
 
• **Incorrect**, as zero work depends on displacement and angle.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: Displacement is zero or perpendicular to force**
 
 
• Zero displacement or perpendicularity between force and displacement results in zero work.
 
• **Correct**, as per the formula W = F × d × cos(θ).

questions.question: If a current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field and the direction of current is reversed, the force on the conductor __________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**reverses direction**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When a **current-carrying conductor** is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force according to the **left-hand rule of Fleming**.
 
• The direction of this force depends on the relative orientation of the current in the conductor and the magnetic field. The force is perpendicular to both the current and the magnetic field.
 
• When the **direction of current** in the conductor is reversed, the force acting on the conductor also reverses its direction. This is because the force is directly proportional to the current direction.
 
• This phenomenon is a direct application of the **Lorentz Force**, which states that the force on a charged particle moving in a magnetic field is given by **F = q(v × B)**, where v represents velocity (current direction in this case).
 
• Hence, reversing the current in the conductor changes the direction of the force acting on it, but the magnitude remains the same. *Hence, the correct answer is that the force reverses direction.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fleming's Left-Hand Rule:**

 
 
• It is used to determine the direction of the force acting on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
 
• The thumb, forefinger, and middle finger of the left hand are stretched perpendicular to each other.
 
• Here, the **thumb** indicates the direction of force, the **forefinger** represents the magnetic field, and the **middle finger** denotes the direction of current.
 
 
 
• **Lorentz Force:**
 
 
• The total force experienced by a charged particle moving in electric and magnetic fields is called the Lorentz force.
 
• The formula for Lorentz force is **F = q(E + v × B)**, where E is the electric field, v is the velocity of the particle, and B is the magnetic field.
 
• In this case, the magnetic component of the Lorentz force is responsible for the force on the conductor.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Force on Current-Carrying Conductors:**
 
 
• This principle is utilized in devices like **electric motors**, where current-carrying coils experience forces in a magnetic field to produce rotational motion.
 
• It is also employed in **magnetic braking systems** and electromagnetic actuators.
 
 
 
• **Magnetic Field and Current Interaction:**
 
 
• The interaction between the magnetic field and current is the basis of many electromechanical devices.
 
• The magnitude of the force can be calculated using the formula **F = I × L × B × sin(θ)**, where I is the current, L is the length of the conductor, B is the magnetic field strength, and θ is the angle between the conductor and the magnetic field.

• **Option 1: Remains the Same:** This is incorrect because reversing the current changes the direction of the force, not leaving it unchanged.
 
• **Option 2: Doubles:** This is incorrect as the magnitude of the force remains the same; only the direction changes.
 
• **Option 3: Reverses Direction:** This is the correct answer as reversing the current causes the force to act in the opposite direction.
 
• **Option 4: Becomes Zero:** This is incorrect because the force only becomes zero if the conductor is parallel to the magnetic field, which is not stated in the question.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct about the 'Attraction of particles of matter'?

options.text: The force of attraction is same for different particles.
The force of attraction is less in liquids as compared to gases.
The force of attraction is more in liquids as compared to solids.
The force of attraction is different for different particles.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The force of attraction is different for different particles.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **force of attraction** between particles of matter varies depending on the state of matter (solid, liquid, or gas). This directly supports the statement that the force of attraction is **different for different particles**.
 
• In **solids**, particles are tightly packed, and the force of attraction is the **strongest**. This is why solids maintain a fixed shape and volume.
 
• In **liquids**, the force of attraction is **weaker** compared to solids, allowing particles to flow and take the shape of their container, while still maintaining a definite volume.
 
• In **gases**, the force of attraction is the **weakest**, as particles are far apart and move freely. Gases neither have a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.
 
• The variation in the force of attraction between particles is the reason for the **different physical properties** of solids, liquids, and gases.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Solids:**

 
 
• In solids, particles are held together by **strong intermolecular forces**.
 
• This strong attraction leads to a **definite shape and volume**.
 
• Examples: **Iron, wood, diamond**.
 
 
 
• **Liquids:**
 
 
• In liquids, particles have a **moderate force of attraction**.
 
• Liquids do not have a fixed shape but have a **definite volume**.
 
• Examples: **Water, oil, alcohol**.
 
 
 
• **Gases:**
 
 
• In gases, particles are held together by **very weak intermolecular forces**.
 
• They neither have a definite shape nor a definite volume, and they expand to fill any container.
 
• Examples: **Oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide**.
 
 
 
• **Plasma:**
 
 
• A state of matter where particles are **ionized**, and the force of attraction is negligible.
 
• Examples: **Sun, lightning**.
 
 
 
• **Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC):**
 
 
• A state of matter formed at **extremely low temperatures**, where particles exhibit unique quantum properties.
 
• It was first observed in **1995** by scientists **Eric Cornell** and **Carl Wieman**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Intermolecular Forces:** These are forces of attraction or repulsion between neighboring particles, including **Van der Waals forces, dipole-dipole interactions, hydrogen bonds,** and others.
 
• **Thermal Energy:** The energy associated with the movement of particles. Higher thermal energy reduces the effect of intermolecular forces, allowing particles to move more freely.
 
• **Phase Transition:** Changes in state (e.g., solid to liquid, liquid to gas) occur due to variations in temperature and pressure, which alter the balance between **intermolecular forces** and thermal energy.
 
• **Applications:** Understanding the force of attraction helps in designing materials, studying fluid dynamics, and even predicting weather patterns.

• Neurons are the structural and functional units of the **nervous system**. They are responsible for processing and transmitting information throughout the body.

• **Signal Transmission:** Neurons communicate via action potentials (electrical signals) and neurotransmitters (chemical signals).
 
• **Nervous System:** Neurons form the foundation of the nervous system, which is divided into the **central nervous system (CNS)** and the **peripheral nervous system (PNS)**.

__
 
• **Ionic compounds are generally soluble in water:** This is due to the polar nature of water molecules. The positive and negative ions in ionic compounds are attracted to the oppositely charged ends of water molecules, leading to their dissolution. Hence, the statement "**Insoluble in water**" is **incorrect**.
 
• **High melting and boiling points:** Ionic compounds have strong electrostatic forces of attraction between their oppositely charged ions, requiring a large amount of energy to break. Hence, statements "**High melting point**" and "**High boiling point**" are **correct**.
 
• **Conductivity in molten state:** Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state or when dissolved in water because their ions become free to move. Hence, the statement "**Conducts electricity in molten state**" is **correct**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Physical Properties of Ionic Compounds:**

 
 
• **Solubility:** Ionic compounds are typically soluble in polar solvents like water but insoluble in non-polar solvents like benzene or ether.
 
• **Conductivity:** In solid-state, ionic compounds do not conduct electricity due to fixed ions. In the molten state or aqueous solution, ions move freely, allowing conductivity.
 
• **Melting and Boiling Points:** Strong ionic bonds result in high melting and boiling points for ionic compounds.
 
• **Hardness:** Ionic compounds are generally hard due to the strong forces holding the ions together. However, they are brittle and can shatter under pressure.

• **Factors Affecting Solubility of Ionic Compounds:**

 
 
• **Lattice Energy:** Higher lattice energy makes it harder for the ionic compound to dissolve in water.
 
• **Hydration Energy:** If the hydration energy of ions is greater than the lattice energy, the compound dissolves easily.
 
 
 
• **Why Ionic Compounds are Brittle:**
 
 
• When a force is applied, the layers of ions shift, causing like charges to align and repel each other, leading to shattering.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Ionic Compounds:**
 
 
• **Sodium chloride:** Used in food preservation and seasoning.
 
• **Calcium carbonate:** Utilized in construction (limestone and marble).
 
• **Magnesium sulfate:** Commonly known as Epsom salt, used in medicine and agriculture.

questions.question: Select the group of organisms in which asexual reproduction occurs by fission.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Blue-green algae**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Blue-green algae**, also known as **cyanobacteria**, reproduce asexually through a process called **binary fission**. This is a simple and efficient method of reproduction where a single cell divides into two identical daughter cells.
 
• In fission, the **genetic material** (DNA) of the parent cell is copied, and the cell divides into two, ensuring that both daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent cell.
 
• Cyanobacteria are **prokaryotic organisms**, meaning they lack a defined nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles, which facilitates their simpler mode of reproduction.
 
• These organisms are found in diverse environments, including **freshwater, marine, and terrestrial ecosystems**. They play a crucial role in ecosystems by contributing to **nitrogen fixation** and oxygen production.
 
• Unlike seed plants and flowering plants, which reproduce sexually, blue-green algae rely on asexual reproduction for their propagation. *Hence, the correct answer is Blue-green algae.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Asexual Reproduction:**

 
 
• Asexual reproduction is a mode of reproduction where offspring are produced from a single organism, and there is no involvement of gametes or sexual processes.
 
• It is commonly observed in **prokaryotes** like bacteria and archaea, as well as in some eukaryotic organisms like fungi, algae, and certain plants and animals.
 
• Common methods of asexual reproduction include **binary fission**, budding, fragmentation, and spore formation.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of Blue-Green Algae (Cyanobacteria):**
 
 
• Cyanobacteria are a group of photosynthetic prokaryotes capable of **oxygenic photosynthesis**, meaning they release oxygen as a byproduct.
 
• They are considered one of the **earliest life forms** on Earth and have played a significant role in shaping the planet’s atmosphere.
 
• Examples include **Oscillatoria, Anabaena, and Nostoc**.
 
• Some cyanobacteria can fix atmospheric nitrogen into a usable form, which is essential for nutrient cycling in ecosystems.
 
 
 
• **Why Other Options Are Incorrect:**
 
 
• **All seed plants:** Seed plants reproduce sexually through the formation of seeds, which involve the fusion of gametes. Asexual reproduction is not a characteristic of all seed plants.
 
• **Flowering plants:** These plants primarily reproduce sexually through flowers, which are specialized structures for sexual reproduction.
 
• **All plants:** While some plants (like algae or mosses) reproduce asexually, not all plants rely on this mode of reproduction. Most higher plants reproduce sexually.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Cyanobacteria:**
 
 
• They are crucial in **aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems** as primary producers.
 
• Cyanobacteria contribute significantly to the **global nitrogen cycle** and are used in biofertilizers to enhance soil fertility.
 
• They are also studied for their potential in **biofuel production** and other biotechnological applications.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Binary Fission:**

 
 
• This is the most common form of asexual reproduction in unicellular organisms.
 
• It involves the replication of the genetic material, followed by the division of the parent cell into two identical cells.
 
• Binary fission is rapid and allows for **exponential population growth** under favorable conditions.
 
 
 
• **Differences Between Asexual and Sexual Reproduction:**
 
 
• **Asexual reproduction:** Involves a single parent, produces genetically identical offspring, and is faster but lacks genetic diversity.
 
• **Sexual reproduction:** Involves two parents, produces genetically diverse offspring, and is slower but enhances adaptability and evolution.
 
 
 
• **Ecological Significance of Cyanobacteria:**
 
 
• Cyanobacteria are crucial in maintaining the balance of oxygen and nutrients in aquatic ecosystems.
 
• They form symbiotic relationships with plants and fungi, aiding in nutrient exchange and ecosystem stability.

questions.question: What are the two main properties of carbon that contribute to its 'versatile nature' and its ability to form a large number of compounds?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Catenation and Tetravalency**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Catenation:** Carbon exhibits a unique ability to form long chains and rings by bonding with other carbon atoms. This property allows the formation of a wide variety of compounds, ranging from simple hydrocarbons to complex organic molecules. The strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms contribute to the stability of these structures.
 
• **Tetravalency:** Carbon has four valence electrons and requires four more electrons to complete its octet. This enables carbon to form four covalent bonds with other atoms (such as hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, etc.) or other carbon atoms, giving rise to a wide range of molecular configurations.
 
• **Versatility in Bond Types:** Carbon can form single, double, and triple bonds, allowing for diverse chemical structures and reactivities. This versatility enables the creation of functional groups and compounds essential for life, such as carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids.
 
• **Formation of Isomers:** Due to its catenation and tetravalency, carbon compounds exhibit isomerism, where molecules with the same molecular formula have different structural arrangements. This adds to the diversity of organic compounds.
 
• **Abundance and Role in Organic Chemistry:** Carbon is a fundamental element in organic chemistry and life. Its ability to form a large number of compounds is a cornerstone in the study of chemistry, biology, and materials science.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Explanation of Catenation:**

 
 
• Catenation is the property of an element to form bonds with atoms of the same element, creating chains or rings. Carbon is exceptional in this regard due to its ability to form strong covalent bonds.
 
• This property is most prominent in carbon compared to other elements like silicon or sulfur, enabling the formation of complex organic molecules.
 
• Examples of catenation include alkanes (single bonds), alkenes (double bonds), and alkynes (triple bonds).
 
 
 
• **Explanation of Tetravalency:**
 
 
• Carbon's tetravalency arises from its electronic configuration (2s² 2p²), where four valence electrons are available for bonding.
 
• This allows carbon to bond with up to four other atoms, leading to the formation of stable molecules like methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆), and ethanol (C₂H₅OH).
 
• Tetravalency enables the creation of diverse molecular geometries, such as linear, planar, and tetrahedral structures.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Elements:**
 
 
• While elements like silicon also exhibit catenation and tetravalency, their bonds are weaker and less stable compared to carbon. This limits their ability to form complex structures.
 
• Carbon's small atomic size and high electronegativity contribute to the strength of its bonds, making it uniquely suited for forming stable, diverse compounds.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Carbon's Properties:**
 
 
• Carbon's versatility is utilized in the synthesis of polymers, fuels, pharmaceuticals, and biomolecules.
 
• Its compounds form the basis of life on Earth, including DNA, RNA, and proteins.
 
• Carbon is also used in materials science to develop substances like graphite, diamond, and carbon nanotubes.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option Analysis:**

 
 
• **Option 1 (High melting point and ductility):** These properties are irrelevant to carbon's versatility. They are more applicable to metals like iron and copper.
 
• **Option 2 (Good conductivity and sonorous nature):** These are metallic properties and do not apply to carbon, which is a non-metal.
 
• **Option 3 (Isomerism and allotropy):** While these are characteristics of carbon, they are a result of its catenation and tetravalency, not the primary reasons for its versatility.
 
• **Option 4 (Catenation and tetravalency):** Correct. These are the two main properties that enable carbon to form a vast number of compounds.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Carbon Compounds:**
 
 
• Simple hydrocarbons: Methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆).
 
• Complex biomolecules: Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆), DNA, proteins.
 
• Industrial compounds: Plastics, synthetic fibers, and fuels.

questions.question: What is the role of the pollen tube in plant fertilisation?

options.text: To produce the male germ cell
To transport pollen grains to the stigma
To transport the male germ cell to the female germ cell

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To transport the male germ cell to the female germ cell**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **pollen tube** is a tubular structure that forms after a pollen grain lands on the stigma of a compatible flower.
 
• Its primary function is to **transport the male germ cell (sperm cells)** from the pollen grain to the ovule, where the female germ cell (egg cell) resides.
 
• The pollen tube grows through the style and into the ovary, navigating to the ovule via a specialized opening called the **micropyle**.
 
• Once the pollen tube reaches the ovule, it releases the sperm cells, enabling the process of fertilization, where one sperm cell fuses with the egg cell to form a **zygote**.
 
• The other sperm cell typically fuses with the central cell to form the **endosperm**, which provides nourishment to the developing embryo.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Pollination**:

 
 
• Pollination is the process of transferring pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower.
 
• It can occur through various agents like wind, water, insects, or animals.
 
• The types of pollination include **self-pollination** (within the same flower or plant) and **cross-pollination** (between flowers of different plants).
 
 
 
• **Fertilization in plants:**
 
 
• Fertilization occurs when the male and female gametes (germ cells) fuse to form a zygote.
 
• This process leads to the formation of seeds, which contain the embryo and endosperm for nourishment.
 
 
 
• **Structure of the pollen tube:**
 
 
• The pollen tube is a microscopic, elongated structure that grows directionally, guided by chemical signals from the ovule.
 
• It has a tip-growing mechanism driven by the cytoskeleton and vesicle trafficking.
 
 
 
• **Micropyle:**
 
 
• The micropyle is a small opening in the ovule through which the pollen tube enters.
 
• It ensures that the sperm cells from the pollen tube reach the egg cell for fertilization.
 
 
 
• **Double fertilization:**
 
 
• Angiosperms exhibit a unique process called double fertilization.
 
• One sperm cell fuses with the egg cell to form a zygote, while the other fuses with two polar nuclei to form the endosperm.
 
• This process ensures both embryo formation and nutrient storage for seed development.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1: To form the zygote**

 
 
• This is incorrect because the formation of the zygote occurs after the sperm and egg cells fuse, not as a role of the pollen tube.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: To produce the male germ cell**
 
 
• This is incorrect as the male germ cells are already present within the pollen grain, not produced by the pollen tube.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: To transport pollen grains to the stigma**
 
 
• This is incorrect because pollen grains are transported to the stigma by pollination agents, not by the pollen tube.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: To transport the male germ cell to the female germ cell**
 
 
• This is correct because the pollen tube facilitates the movement of sperm cells to the ovule for fertilization.

__
 
• **Unbalanced Force:** An unbalanced force occurs when the net force acting on an object is not zero, causing a change in the object's state of motion (either speed, direction, or both).
 
• **Correct Option Explanation:** A ball rolling on the ground and eventually stopping involves an unbalanced force because friction acts as an opposing force, slowing down the ball until it comes to rest.
 
• **Frictional Force:** The friction between the ball and the ground is the unbalanced force responsible for reducing the ball's motion and eventually bringing it to a stop.
 
• **Newton's First Law:** According to Newton's First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia), an object in motion will remain in motion unless acted upon by an external unbalanced force. The rolling ball's motion changes due to the unbalanced frictional force, making the situation fit this law.
 
• **Other Options:** In the other scenarios provided (standing person, car moving at uniform speed, book on a table), the forces acting on the objects are balanced, meaning their state of motion remains unchanged. These are not examples of unbalanced forces.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Balanced Forces:**

 
 
• Balanced forces occur when the net force acting on an object is zero, meaning no change in the object's motion occurs.
 
• Examples include a person standing still on the ground (gravity and normal force cancel each other out) or a book resting on a table.
 
 
 
• **Unbalanced Forces:**
 
 
• Unbalanced forces result in a net force on an object, leading to a change in its motion (acceleration or deceleration).
 
• Examples include a rolling ball slowing down due to friction or a car accelerating forward when a greater force is applied by the engine than the opposing frictional forces.
 
 
 
• **Friction:**
 
 
• Friction is a force that opposes the relative motion of two surfaces in contact.
 
• It is a critical factor in real-world scenarios, as it often acts as the unbalanced force responsible for changes in motion.
 
 
 
• **Newton's Laws of Motion:**
 
 
• **First Law:** An object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force.
 
• **Second Law:** The force acting on an object is equal to the mass of the object multiplied by its acceleration (**F = ma**).
 
• **Third Law:** For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Friction and Motion:** Friction is essential for activities such as walking or driving, as it provides the necessary grip for movement. However, it also opposes motion, requiring additional force to maintain movement.
 
• **Types of Friction:**
 
 
• **Static Friction:** Acts on objects at rest, preventing them from starting to move.
 
• **Kinetic Friction:** Acts on moving objects, opposing their motion.
 
• **Rolling Friction:** Specific to rolling objects, like a ball or wheel, and typically lower than sliding friction.
 
 
 
• **Applications:** Understanding unbalanced forces is crucial in designing vehicles, machines, and other systems where motion control is essential.
 
• **Real-Life Example:** A bicycle slowing down when the rider stops pedaling is another instance of an unbalanced force (friction and air resistance) acting to reduce motion.

questions.question: Which incident was responsible for the beginning of the Chipko Movement in the village of Reni?

options.text: Sale of forest by local residents
Approval given to a contractor to fell trees near the village
Government decision to use forest land for farming

questions.solution: The correct answer is __**Approval given to a contractor to fell trees near the village**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** • The **Chipko Movement**, a historic environmental movement in India, began in the **village of Reni** in the Garhwal Himalayas of **Uttarakhand** in **1973**. • The movement was triggered when the government approved a **contract to a sports goods company** to fell trees in the forests near the village of Reni. • When the men of the village were away, the **women of Reni**, led by **Gaura Devi**, organized themselves to protect the trees by physically hugging them, preventing the contractors from cutting them down. • This act of hugging the trees, symbolizing a non-violent protest, drew significant attention to the environmental degradation caused by deforestation and highlighted the need for sustainable forest management. • The Chipko Movement is considered one of the earliest and most successful environmental movements in India and inspired similar movements across the country.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Right-hand thumb rule gives the direction of magnetic field around a straight conductor.
Right-hand thumb rule cannot be applied to circular loops.
Right-hand thumb rule cannot be applied to a straight conductor.
Right-hand thumb rule can be used to find the force on a conductor in a magnetic field.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Right-hand thumb rule gives the direction of magnetic field around a straight conductor.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Right-hand thumb rule:** This rule is used to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor. If the thumb of the right hand points in the direction of the current, the curled fingers show the direction of the magnetic field lines. *This statement is correct.*
 
• **Application to circular loops:** The right-hand thumb rule is applicable to circular loops as well. Here, the thumb points in the direction of the current, and the fingers show the direction of the magnetic field along the circular path. Hence, the claim that it cannot be applied to circular loops is *incorrect.*
 
• **Application to straight conductors:** The rule is specifically meant for straight conductors, making the claim that it cannot be applied to straight conductors *incorrect.*
 
• **Finding force on a conductor:** The right-hand thumb rule is not used to determine the force on a conductor. Instead, the Fleming’s left-hand rule is applied for this purpose. Hence, this statement is *incorrect.*
 
• **Correct statement:** The right-hand thumb rule accurately gives the direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor. This is a fundamental concept in electromagnetism. *Hence, option 1 is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Right-hand thumb rule:**

 
 
• The rule was introduced to understand the relationship between current and magnetic fields in a conductor.
 
• It states: "If you hold a current-carrying conductor in your right hand such that the thumb points in the direction of the current, the direction of your curled fingers will indicate the direction of the magnetic field lines."
 
• This rule is derived from Maxwell's right-hand grip rule.
 
 
 
• **Magnetic field around a conductor:**
 
 
• When current flows through a conductor, it generates a magnetic field around it.
 
• The field lines form concentric circles around the conductor, and their direction is determined using the right-hand thumb rule.
 
 
 
• **Fleming's left-hand rule:**
 
 
• This rule is used to determine the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
 
• According to this rule, if the thumb, forefinger, and middle finger of the left hand are stretched mutually perpendicular to each other:
 
 
• The thumb points in the direction of force (motion).
 
• The forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field.
 
• The middle finger points in the direction of the current.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Applications:**
 
 
• The right-hand thumb rule is widely used in designing electrical devices like motors, generators, and transformers.
 
• It helps engineers understand how magnetic fields interact with electric currents to produce motion or induce current.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Hans Christian Ørsted:** The discovery of the magnetic effect of electric current was made by **Hans Christian Ørsted** in **1820**. This discovery formed the basis of electromagnetism.
 
• **Magnetic field strength:** The strength of the magnetic field generated by a current-carrying conductor depends on:
 
 
• The amount of current flowing through the conductor.
 
• The distance from the conductor; the field weakens as the distance increases.
 
 
 
• **Practical examples:** The right-hand thumb rule is applied in understanding the functioning of solenoids, electromagnets, and electric motors.
 
• **Conceptual difference:** While the right-hand thumb rule is used to determine the magnetic field direction, the Fleming’s left-hand rule is used to determine force direction, and the Fleming’s right-hand rule is used to find the direction of induced current.

questions.question: Which of the following options is INCORRECT regarding when rate of evaporation increases?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Increase in humidity**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Evaporation** is the process through which a liquid changes into a gas at a temperature below its boiling point.
 
• Evaporation is influenced by several factors such as **temperature, surface area, wind speed, and humidity**.
 
• **Increase in temperature:** Higher temperatures provide more energy to liquid molecules, making it easier for them to escape into the gaseous phase. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• **Increase in surface area:** A larger surface area allows more liquid to be exposed to the air, facilitating faster evaporation. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• **Increase in wind speed:** Faster winds remove water vapor from the surface, reducing humidity near the liquid and enhancing evaporation. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• **Increase in humidity:** Higher humidity means more water vapor is already present in the air, making it harder for additional liquid to evaporate. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Evaporation and its Importance:**

 
 
• Evaporation plays a key role in the **water cycle**, contributing to cloud formation and precipitation.
 
• It is also critical in cooling mechanisms such as **sweating**, which helps regulate body temperature.
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting Evaporation:**
 
 
• **Temperature:** Higher temperatures increase molecular kinetic energy, leading to faster evaporation.
 
• **Surface Area:** A larger surface area provides more opportunities for molecules to escape into the air.
 
• **Wind Speed:** Wind removes saturated air near the liquid's surface, increasing the evaporation rate.
 
• **Humidity:** Higher humidity slows evaporation as the air is already saturated with water vapor.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Evaporation:**
 
 
• Used in industries such as **salt production** through seawater evaporation.
 
• Evaporation helps in cooling systems like **air coolers** and refrigeration.
 
 
 
• **Real-World Examples:**
 
 
• Clothes dry faster in **dry and windy weather** due to faster evaporation.
 
• Evaporation from oceans and lakes contributes to the formation of **rain clouds**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Evaporation vs Boiling:**

 
 
• **Evaporation** occurs at any temperature below the boiling point and only at the surface of the liquid.
 
• **Boiling** occurs at a fixed temperature (boiling point) and throughout the liquid.
 
 
 
• **Role of Humidity:**
 
 
• **High humidity:** Reduces the evaporation rate because the air is nearly saturated with water vapor.
 
• **Low humidity:** Increases evaporation since the air can absorb more water vapor.
 
 
 
• **Scientific Insight:** Evaporation is an endothermic process, meaning it absorbs heat from the surroundings, resulting in a cooling effect.
